title: Bank Earnings Kick Off Mixed: JPMorgan Misses, Citi and Goldman Beat
excerpt: JPMorgan posted its first earnings miss in 17 quarters as expenses climbed 12%, while Goldman Sachs rode a trading surge to the second-best revenue quarter in its history and Citigroup delivered its strongest third-quarter revenue in a decade.
body:
• JPMorgan missed Wall Street estimates for the first time in 17 quarters: EPS of $5.57, or $5.75 excluding an investment-securities loss, against $5.93 expected, on reported revenue of $50.17 billion versus $51.23 billion forecast.
  • Goldman Sachs crushed expectations with EPS of $17.01 against a consensus near $13.09, as equities trading revenue surged 72% and net revenue of $18.68 billion made it the second-best quarter in the firm's history.
  • Citigroup beat with EPS of $2.85 and its best third-quarter revenue in a decade at $23.85 billion, yet its shares fell 5.6% as investors focused on credit costs.
  • Johnson & Johnson raised its full-year guidance after sales grew 5.9% to $25.40 billion, with adjusted EPS of $2.59.

Third-quarter earnings season opened Tuesday with a split verdict from America's biggest banks. JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, missed analyst estimates for the first time in 17 quarters as a securities loss and fast-rising expenses ate into its results. Goldman Sachs, by contrast, turned a volatile trading quarter into the second-biggest revenue haul in its history, and Citigroup posted its strongest third-quarter revenue in a decade — though investors sold its shares anyway.

JPMorgan's rare miss

JPMorgan reported net income of $15.3 billion, up 6% from a year earlier, with diluted earnings of $5.57 a share. A $658 million net loss on investment securities weighed on the quarter; excluding it, earnings were $5.75 a share, still short of the $5.93 consensus compiled by FactSet. Reported revenue came to $50.17 billion, below the $51.23 billion analysts expected, according to Investor's Business Daily.

Two pressure points explain the shortfall. Expenses climbed 12% to $27.3 billion, outpacing revenue growth as the bank spent on front-office hiring, technology and wage inflation. Fixed-income trading revenue fell 4% to $5.4 billion, missing forecasts by roughly $550 million. The rest of the machine performed: equities revenue jumped 49%, investment banking fees rose 14% to $3.0 billion, and net interest income grew 13% to about $27.1 billion. Consumer and community banking revenue rose 9%, evidence that US households and businesses are still spending and borrowing.

Chief Executive Jamie Dimon said in the release that the economy continues to be fueled by strong business investment and consumer spending, while flagging large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices and rising interest rates as forces building under the surface — and that the bank remains prepared for a wide range of outcomes. On the earnings call, he warned that financial pain across the US would worsen if interest rates climb another percentage point.

Goldman's blowout quarter

Goldman Sachs reported diluted EPS of $17.01, far above the consensus of roughly $13.09, on net revenues of $18.68 billion — up 23% from a year earlier and the second-highest quarterly total in the firm's history, according to its third-quarter earnings release. Net earnings were $5.29 billion, and annualized return on common equity reached 18.7%.

Equities trading did the heavy lifting: revenue there surged 72% to $6.44 billion as volatile markets, whipsawed by energy prices and shifting rate expectations, kept clients trading. Global Banking & Markets revenue rose 32% to $13.46 billion, and investment banking fees climbed 21% to $3.22 billion on stronger advisory and underwriting work. Fixed income, currencies and commodities was the soft spot, roughly flat at $3.47 billion.

"Our clients continued to turn to Goldman Sachs for our world-class advice, execution and financing capabilities, resulting in our second highest quarterly net revenues."

— David Solomon, Chairman and CEO, Goldman Sachs

Citi beats, shares sink

Citigroup earned $2.85 a share against a $2.65 consensus, as net income jumped about 40% to $5.2 billion. Revenue rose 8% to $23.85 billion — the bank's best third quarter in a decade, as Chief Executive Jane Fraser noted in the release — with services revenue up 15% to $6.61 billion and markets revenue up 6% to $6.11 billion. Costs fell, improving the efficiency ratio to 58.5% from 64.7% a year earlier.

Investors were not impressed. Citi shares reversed an early gain to fall 5.6% on the day, with traders focusing on a 4% decline in non-interest revenue, rising credit provisions and the bank's exposure to Mexican credit. The reaction summed up the day's mood: solid headline numbers were not enough to overcome questions about credit quality and costs.

Beyond the banks: J&J, Wells Fargo, UnitedHealth

Johnson & Johnson, reporting the same morning, grew sales 5.9% to $25.40 billion, driven by a 7.7% rise in Innovative Medicine revenue to $16.76 billion, while MedTech sales rose 2.5% to $8.64 billion. Adjusted earnings were $2.59 a share; reported EPS of $0.09 reflected a one-time special charge tied to a proposed talc litigation resolution and recent acquisitions. The company raised its full-year guidance in its results release, lifting expected reported sales to $101.2 billion at the midpoint and adjusted EPS guidance by $0.06 to $11.10 at the midpoint.

Wells Fargo posted EPS of $1.87, a shade above the $1.85 expected, but revenue of $21.87 billion came in light and its shares fell about 3%. UnitedHealth beat more cleanly: adjusted EPS of $4.69 against a $4.14 average estimate on lower-than-feared medical costs, and the insurer raised its 2026 adjusted profit outlook to at least $20.50 a share, according to Reuters.

What to watch next

The split opening sets the season's themes. Trading desks are thriving on volatility and consumers are still spending, but expenses and credit costs are rising just as interest rates climb again — the Federal Reserve raised rates in September for the first time in three years, and markets expect more tightening. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report on Wednesday, and investors will press on the same two points: whether cost growth keeps outrunning revenue, and whether credit provisions keep building.

For investors holding bank stocks in brokerage or retirement accounts, the immediate takeaway is narrow but useful: the sector's earnings engine is intact, yet the market is now punishing cost growth and credit slippage faster than it rewards revenue beats.
